verses.1: Al-Mizan explains ḍuḥāhā as the spreading sunshine and unfolding day, hence the forenoon. The feminine pronoun is the sun, and the oath includes its light extending over the earth.
verses.2: Al-Mizan takes the moon's following of the sun to mean either its reception of the sun's light, a constant fact, or its rising after sunset during the lunar month's first half, from crescent to full moon.
verses.3: Al-Mizan reads tajliyah as manifesting: the day makes the earth visible, so the feminine pronoun refers to the earth. It rejects readings that make the day reveal the sun, since the sun rather reveals the day, and considers the alternatives of the world, darkness, or God revealing the sun unlikely.
verses.4: Al-Mizan identifies the object covered by night as the earth and its objects, not the sun. The shift from the past jallāhā to the present yaghshāhā subtly evokes Islam's early appearance amid an earth covered by vice and transgression; the form also preserves the surrounding rhyme.
verses.5: Al-Mizan takes mā in the oaths by the sky and earth as referring to God, whose ambiguity conveys glorification and wonder, while ṭaḥw means stretching or extending. It rejects taking mā as a verbal-noun particle, because the parallel oath concerning the soul and its fashioning supports the relative reading.

verses.7: Al-Mizan understands the oath as by the human soul in its absolute sense and by its wise Fashioner. The indefinite nafs glorifies such a soul rather than merely leaving it unspecified; restricting it to Adam lacks support and clashes with the ensuing address to the soul, except through an implausible istikhdām. Ilhām is God's casting a concept or judgment into the soul: He gives it practical reason to discern the categories of virtue and vice, not merely the outward forms of acts. Fujūr is tearing the veil of divine prohibition, while taqwā is self-protection through avoiding the prohibited, identified in narrations with waraʿ. Thus this created discernment concerns the human soul, and by implication jinn subject to obligation. An editor's note adds that the commentary treats value-predicates as mental abstractions rather than qualities in external reality. Falāḥ is attaining one's aim and khaybah its opposite; tazkiyah is fostering the soul's sound growth, whereas tadassī is covertly forcing it against its intended disposition. The soul's fiṭrah recognizes submission to God as its proper course: Godwariness fosters it, while immersion in vice frustrates its healthy growth.

verses.11: Al-Mizan presents Thamūd's denial through bi-ṭaghwāhā—rebellion or transgression—as evidence confirming that the soul prospers or fails according to how it is fostered. The narrations name Qudār b. Sālif as the man who hamstrung the she-camel, while the following plural pronouns show that his people instigated him.

verses.13: Al-Mizan identifies God's messenger as Ṣāliḥ, prophet to Thamūd. He warned them to leave God's she-camel unharmed and allow her to drink, rather than kill her or prevent her access to water.
verses.14: Al-Mizan explains ʿaqr as striking at the root and thus killing the camel, and damdamah as a crushing punishment that annihilated Thamūd's progeny and effaced their traces for their sin. It most plausibly takes the feminine pronoun in fa-sawwāhā as Thamūd, a feminine qabīlah, so that their town was razed; it also reports readings referring to the leveled earth or to an indiscriminate obliteration.
verses.15: Al-Mizan takes the pronoun to refer to the preceding obliteration or leveling: God does not fear its aftermath as rulers fear retaliation, for affairs end according to His plan. It rejects readings that make the fearless subject the camel-killer or Ṣāliḥ.
